# How to Move Your Lips When Kissing (Catch, Hold, Release) Nobody moves their lips when they kiss. Strange thing to read in an article with this title, I know. Stay with me, because the phrase you just typed into a search bar is the exact thing standing between you and a better kiss. "Move your lips" suggests motion across a surface. Sliding. Gliding. Some continuous buffing action you're supposed to be performing and clearly aren't. That mental image has wrecked more kisses than bad breath ever has, and I know because I spent most of one summer at nineteen doing what I can only describe as polishing someone's mouth. Lips don't slide. They close. Yours gather up one of theirs, hold for a beat, and let go. Then again, slightly differently. Catch, hold, release. That's the whole engine, and everything below is a variation on those three beats. ## How to move your lips when kissing, in one paragraph Close your lips softly around one of theirs, usually their lower lip. Hold for one to two seconds. Release, separating only a few millimeters. Change one small thing (pressure, angle, or which lip you take) and do it again. Your lips stay relaxed and barely parted the entire time, never puckered tight and never pressed flat. The motion is a slow open-and-close, not a side-to-side slide, and the two of you alternate rather than moving in unison. That's the mechanic. The rest of this explains why it works, how to get loose enough to do it, and the six ways people get it wrong. ## Why the phrase move your lips ruins kisses Ask the internet what to do with your lips and you get the same four words in ninety different fonts: relax and follow their lead. Which is like teaching someone to drive by telling them to feel the road. Accurate. Utterly unusable. When you're three inches from someone's face with your pulse in your ears, "relax" isn't an instruction. It's a wish. Nobody gets specific because the mechanic is genuinely hard to put into words. We all learned it by accident, from someone who also learned it by accident, and afterward none of us can explain it. The advice defaults to vibes instead, and you're left assuming there's some motion everyone else figured out and you missed. There isn't. There's a grip. ## The one-lip rule that fixes almost everything Here's what nobody tells you, and it's the most useful sentence in this article: You kiss one lip at a time. Not their mouth. One lip. Usually the bottom one, because it's fuller, easier to catch, and taking it leaves their top lip free to do the same thing to yours. Think about a wooden joint. Two flat boards pressed face to face aren't joined, they're just touching. A joint happens when one piece *takes* the other. Mouths work the same way. Two full sets of lips mashed flat together have nothing to hold and nowhere to go, and that is the kiss people describe as mushy. Mushy is almost never a wetness problem. It's an alignment problem. Offset yourself, then. [Tilt your head](/blog/why-do-we-tilt-our-heads-when-we-kiss/) enough that your mouths land at an angle instead of dead-on, and let your lips settle around their lower lip while their upper lip rests in the dip of yours. Now you're interlocked. Now there's something there to actually kiss. Want to feel the movement right now, with nobody present? Close your lips gently around your own fingertip, the way you'd pick up a grape without bruising it. That soft, deliberate gathering is the entire motion. That's it. That's the thing you've been trying to reverse-engineer. ## Catch, hold, release: the three beats ### The catch Your lips arrive relaxed and slightly parted, then close around their lip. Gently. The pressure is roughly what you'd use to hold a contact lens, not what you'd use to check whether a peach is ripe. And it's a closing motion, which means it comes from your whole mouth softening around something, not from your lips pushing forward at it. Pushing forward is puckering. Puckering is the enemy, and it gets its own section. ### The hold This is the beat everybody skips, and skipping it is why so many kisses feel frantic. Once you've caught their lip, stay. One second. Two. Do nothing at all. It feels much longer from the inside than it looks from the outside, and it does most of the emotional work of the kiss, because holding still reads as certainty while hurrying reads as nerves. There's a physical reason too: [your lips carry an absurd density of nerve endings](/blog/why-lips-are-so-sensitive/), so the sensation arrives instantly but keeps unfolding for several seconds after. Leave early and you both got the headline without the story. If you take one thing from this article, take the hold. ### The release Let go slowly, and separate barely. A few millimeters, not a few inches. You aren't ending the kiss, you're resetting it. The release is where you breathe, where you change the angle, and where the anticipation quietly rebuilds itself. Then you catch again with one small thing different. Catch, hold, release. Catch, hold, release. Once you feel that pulse, kissing stops being something you're performing and starts being something you're *doing*.

The catch-hold-release pulse is the foundation every other move in Kiss Perfect Now is built on top of.

See what's inside →
## The pucker problem, and how to unclench Almost every stiff kiss traces back to one source: lips pushed forward and held tight. The kiss emoji. The face you make for an aunt. A pucker is a hard surface. It can't gather, it can't close around anything, and it reduces your mouth to a small firm object being applied to someone's face. You cannot fix pressure, rhythm, or angle while you're puckered, because a puckered mouth doesn't have those settings. Three physical cues that unlock it: - **Unhinge your jaw slightly.** Let it hang. A clenched jaw pulls your lips tight automatically, and nearly everyone clenches the instant they get nervous. - **Park your tongue.** Rest it low and loose behind your bottom teeth. Pressing it to the roof of your mouth tenses everything above it. ([Where it goes after that is a longer conversation.](/blog/where-to-put-your-tongue-when-kissing/)) - **Say the word huh, then freeze.** Say it out loud and stop your mouth exactly where it lands: barely parted, completely slack. That's the shape your lips want to be in when they arrive. Softness is also, unglamorously, a maintenance question. Nobody enjoys catching sandpaper. [Twenty seconds of upkeep](/blog/how-to-make-your-lips-soft-for-kissing/) handles it. ## Five ways to vary the beat Once the pulse is running, you vary it. One dial at a time. Turning all five at once reads as panic. - **Pressure.** Firmer for two beats, then back to barely there. Contrast is the whole game. - **Which lip.** Take their bottom lip three times, then take the top one. That switch feels enormous from the other side and costs you nothing. - **Angle.** Come back five degrees off from where you left. New angle, new kiss. - **Duration.** A long hold, then a fast one, then another long one. A predictable tempo is the quickest route to forgettable. - **The drag.** On the release, keep your lips closed half a second too long so their lip slips slowly out of them. It's the closest thing to genuine movement in this entire article, and it works because it's rare, not because it's constant. There's a sixth, which is [catching their lip with the very edge of your teeth](/blog/lip-biting-while-kissing/). Use it once in a while. It's a punchline, not a paragraph. ## Do you both move your lips at the same time? No. This is the question I get more than any other, and the answer is genuinely counterintuitive. You alternate. When you catch, they hold. When you release, they catch. It's turn-taking, for the same reason two people talking at once produces noise instead of a conversation. Nobody negotiates this out loud. You fall into it by paying attention to them rather than auditing yourself, and when both of you kiss simultaneously you get that flat, effortful feeling where plenty is happening and none of it is landing. The fix takes exactly one kiss. Go still and let them lead for a few beats. Feel their tempo. Then start answering it. [Matching someone's rhythm](/blog/how-to-match-your-partners-kissing-style/) is most of what people actually mean when they call somebody a good kisser, and it's the difference between two people kissing and two people taking turns being kissed. If your brain won't quiet down long enough to notice any of this, that's a separate and very fixable problem. [Overthinking mid-kiss](/blog/how-to-stop-overthinking-when-you-kiss/) has ruined more first kisses than bad technique ever managed. ## What your lips should never do - **The flat press.** Both mouths dead-on, full contact, no grip anywhere. This is the mush. - **The vacuum.** Sucking. Your lips close; they don't inhale. If it's audible, it's too much. - **The machine gun.** Six rapid pecks in a row. No hold, no release, just repeated arrival. - **The wander.** Sliding side to side across their mouth searching for something. There's nothing to find out there. Catch instead. - **The lick.** Wetting their lips for them is a coin flip on a good day, and it's the express lane to [a saliva problem](/blog/too-much-saliva-when-kissing/). - **The statue.** Lips arrive, lips remain, nothing else occurs for nine seconds. A hold is a beat. It is not the whole song. Every one of these turns up on [the list of things that make someone a bad kisser](/blog/signs-youre-a-bad-kisser/), and every one comes from the same root: trying to move instead of trying to close. ## The part the mechanic cannot teach you I've just handed you a grip, three beats, five dials, and six failure modes, and I want to be straight with you about what all of it is for. It's scaffolding. It exists to give your attention somewhere to go besides worry. Because the reason the hold works isn't mechanical at all. Staying still for two full seconds with your mouth on someone else's is a small act of nerve. It says you're not rushing and you're not going anywhere, and that is the actual message being sent. The mechanic is only how it gets delivered. Run the beats until they're automatic. [Twenty minutes of deliberate attention](/blog/how-to-practice-kissing/) will do it, which is a laughable investment for a skill you'll use for the rest of your life. [The research on why kissing works on us](/blog/science-of-kissing/) is fascinating, but no study has ever improved anyone's kiss. Reps do. Then forget every word of this and pay attention to the person instead. Your lips will sort themselves out. They always could. They just needed permission to stop trying to move. ## Frequently Asked Questions ### How do you move your lips when kissing for the first time? Keep it simple: close your lips gently around their lower lip, hold for a beat or two, and release without pulling far away. Repeat with slightly different pressure or angle. Do not attempt to slide, and do not pucker. A soft catch and an unhurried hold is a genuinely good first kiss, and it beats anything more elaborate. ### Do you move your lips at the same time as the other person? No, you alternate. When you close around their lip, they should be holding still; when you release, it becomes their turn. Kissing in unison creates the flat, mashed feeling where both people are working hard and nothing registers. If you lose the rhythm, go still for a few beats, let them lead, then answer. ### Should your lips be open or closed when kissing? Barely parted. Fully closed lips can't catch anything and turn the kiss into a press, while a wide-open mouth is overwhelming without tongue involvement to justify it. The target is the relaxed, slightly separated shape your mouth naturally makes when your jaw is loose, which is also what lets you close softly around their lip. ### Why does my kissing feel stiff or awkward? Almost always the pucker. Lips pushed forward and held tense cannot gather, vary pressure, or change angle, so the kiss has nowhere to develop. Unclench your jaw, rest your tongue low behind your bottom teeth, and let your lips go slack before you make contact. Stiffness is muscle tension, not a lack of skill. ### How do you move your lips when kissing a guy? Identically. Lip mechanics are not gendered: catch, hold, release, and vary one thing at a time. The only pattern worth knowing is that men are more often kissed at a faster tempo than they'd choose, so slowing down and adding a real two-second hold tends to land harder than anything else you could do. ### How hard should you press your lips when kissing? Light to start, then vary it. Begin at roughly the pressure you'd use to hold a contact lens and build from there based on how they respond. The important part isn't the amount, it's the change: alternating between firm and feather-light for a few beats is what makes a kiss feel alive rather than uniform.
